segments.text: Big idea. The 70 weeks, 490 prophetic years, are severed,
khatach, from the 2300 day timeline, anchoring the entire prophetic calendar in the historical
decree of 457 BC. This reading finds that Jesus Christ arrived and died on the prophetic
schedule in AD 31, and it carries the remaining 1,810 years to 1844 on the same line.
In plain words, Daniel 9 gives the 70 weeks, as 490 years, from the decree to rebuild Jerusalem
to the coming of the Messiah, and the cross falls in the middle of the last week.
From the last sitting, sitting 8. In sitting 8, Daniel received the longest time prophecy in the
Bible. Unto 2300 days, then shall the sanctuary be cleansed, Daniel 8.14. The Hebrew nitzdak means
put right. But Gabriel's explanation was cut short. Daniel fainted and was six certain days,
and none understood the vision. Daniel 8.27. The 2300 days in that chapter have no starting point.
Chapter 9 opens years later, in 538 BC. The Babylonian empire has fallen to Medo-Persia,
Daniel is studying Jeremiah's 70-year prophecy of the exile. And while he pours out his heart
in sackcloth and ashes, Gabriel suddenly reappears to complete the explanation he began at the River
Uli. Introduction. Daniel's penitential prayer and Gabriel's return. Daniel 9, 1-4, 20-23, Babylon,
538 BC. In the first year of Darius the Mede, 538 BC, Daniel was studying the books of the
prophet Jeremiah. He understood by the books that the desolation of Jerusalem would accomplish 70
literal years. Daniel 9, 1-2, Jeremiah 25, 11-12, 29-10. Since the first deportation
occurred in 605 BC, approximately 67 years had elapsed. The end of the exile was drawing near.
Yet Daniel did not passively wait. Deeply concerned that the sins of his people might
prolong their captivity, he set his face toward the Lord God. To seek by prayer,
supplications, fasting, sackcloth, and ashes, Daniel 9, 3. Daniel's intercessory prayer,
Daniel 9, verses 4-19, is one of the most sublime confessions in Scripture.
Though his accusers found no fault in his administration, he confessed his own sin
with his peoples and repeatedly identified himself with the transgressions of his nation.
We have sinned and have committed iniquity and have done wickedly and have rebelled,
Daniel 9, 5. While Daniel was still speaking in prayer, presenting his supplication for the
holy mountain of God, the angel Gabriel, whom he had seen in the vision at the beginning,
Daniel 8, 16, flew swiftly and touched him about the time of the evening sacrifice,
Daniel 9, 20-21. Gabriel announced his divine mission.
O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding. At the beginning of
thy supplications, the commandment came forth, and I am come to show thee,
for thou art greatly beloved. Therefore, understand the matter and consider the vision.
Daniel 9, 22-23. Notice Gabriel's command. Consider the vision. What vision?
In Daniel 9, no new symbolic beasts or horns appear. The only vision under discussion is the
unexplained 2300 day vision of Daniel 8, which had caused Daniel to faint and remain sick for
Daniel 8, 27. Gabriel has returned specifically to unlock that very timeline.
Main point 1. The Hebrew verb chatak, severed from the 2300 days. Daniel 9, 24.
Gabriel immediately begins his explanation by revealing the first portion of the timeline.
70 weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city,
to finish the transgression and to make an end of sins and to make reconciliation
for iniquity and to bring in everlasting righteousness and to seal up the vision
and prophecy and to anoint the Most Holy. Daniel 9, 24.
A week, Hebrew Shabuah, literally means a unit of seven. 70 weeks equals 70 times seven,
which is 490 prophetic days. Numbers 14, 34 and Ezekiel 4, 6 appoint each day for a year.
In plain words, in this kind of prophecy, one day stands for one year of real history.
Read that way, the 490 days are 490 literal solar years set apart for Daniel's people and for
Jerusalem. Daniel 9, 24 names six goals for those weeks, to finish the transgression,
to make an end of sins, to make reconciliation for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness,
to seal up the vision and prophecy and to anoint the Most Holy.
On this reading, the first four are met by what Christ does on the cross,
where Messiah is cut off for others and the sacrifices stop. The last two fit the sealing
or confirming of the vision when it is fulfilled and the anointing of the Most Holy,
which this reading ties to Christ's anointing at his baptism.
The vision was shut up. In Daniel 8, 26, the angel said,
shut thou up the vision, for it shall be for many days.
It was shut because the 2300 days had no starting point. Daniel 9, 24 says the weeks
are given to seal up the vision and prophecy, that is, to settle the matter by explaining it.
So on this reading, the 70 weeks are the answer to the question Daniel was left with.
They supply the start the 2300 days were missing.
A reader can check the claim. Chapter 8 gives a number and no date,
and Chapter 9 is where the date is given.
A word used only once, khatach, means cut.
The English King James version translates the Hebrew verb as determined,
Daniel 9, 24. However, the inspired word is khatach,
a word that appears only once in the entire Hebrew Old Testament,
which scholars call a hapax lagaminon.
Later Hebrew and related languages often use khatach for cutting or dividing.
Its basic meaning is properly to cut, to divide, hence to decree, to determine.
Khatach means cut off. The 490 years are cut from the 2300 year line of Daniel 8, 14,
joining the two chapters on one start. Khatach means, quote,
properly to cut, to divide, hence to decree, to determine.
Rabbinic usage. Khatach is used for cutting off a piece of flesh or trimming a vine.
From what are the 70 weeks, 490 years, cut off?
They cannot be cut from empty space.
They are cut from the only longer time prophecy that Gabriel was sent to explain,
the 2300 day vision of Daniel 8, 14.
Daniel 8, 14 says 2300 days, and this reading counts them as years.
By the same day for a year rule, it uses for the 490.
The lexicon gives cut as the root sense of khatach,
and decree or determine as a sense that grew from it.
And the King James version shows determined.
This reading keeps the root sense because Gabriel is explaining a vision
whose length is already given, so the weeks are a piece of it.
Gabriel states a starting point for the weeks,
Daniel 9, 25, and none for the 2300.
So this reading takes the 490 years to be the first part of the 2300.
The command in Daniel 9, 23 was to consider the vision Daniel had not understood,
Daniel 8, 27, and a piece cut from the front of that longer span
would carry the start the vision was missing.
Both then start at the same place in history.
The verse does not print that step.
It is this reading's inference from Gabriel's command,
from the length already given in Daniel 8, 14,
and from the missing date in Daniel 8.
Main point two.
Four Persian decrees, identifying the 457 BC anchor.
Daniel 9, 25, Ezra 7, 11, through 26.
Gabriel provides the precise historical event that triggers the countdown.
Know therefore and understand that from the going forth of the commandment
to restore and to build Jerusalem unto the Messiah the Prince
shall be seven weeks and threescore in two weeks.
The street shall be built again and the wall even in troubleless times.
Daniel 9, 25, KJV.
Persian monarchs issued several royal commissions regarding the Jewish return.
Bible students often compare three restoring decrees.
Cyrus, Darius, Artaxerxes.
This sighting adds Nehemiah's wall commission as a fourth line on the chart.
A permit under Artaxerxes, not a new charter for Daniel 9, 25.
Persian commissions compared.
Three decrees plus Nehemiah permit.
One.
The decree of Cyrus the Great, 538 to 537 BC, Ezra 1 to 4.
Cyrus authorized the exiles to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.
It contained no authorization to restore municipal self-government,
appoint judges, or rebuild the civil city.
Two.
The decree of Darius I, Histopeses, 520 BC, Ezra 6, 1 to 12.
When Samaritan adversaries halted temple construction,
Darius confirmed Cyrus's original edict.
This was purely a reaffirmation of temple rebuilding,
adding no civil or administrative authority.
Three.
The decree of Artaxerxes, the first longuminous.
Autumn 457 BC, Ezra 7, 11 to 26.
In the seventh year of his reign,
Artaxerxes sent Ezra the scribe a royal order called a firman.
It gave Ezra full civil authority to appoint magistrates and judges
to teach and enforce the laws of God and the king,
and to punish by death, banishment, confiscation of goods, or imprisonment.
Ezra 7, 25 to 26.
This reading takes it to be the only decree that both restored the Jews' own government
and led to the rebuilding of the city of Jerusalem.
The sign that building went on under it is Ezra 412,
where officials complain that the Jews who came up from Artaxerxes are
building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls thereof.
Four.
The commission to Nehemiah, 444 BC, Nehemiah 2, 1 to 8.
In his 20th year, Artaxerxes granted Nehemiah personal permission
and timber to rebuild the physical walls of Jerusalem.
This was a permit to finish the walls under the existing 457 BC decree.
It gave Nehemiah timber and royal backing,
but it did not give the Jews a new government
because the 457 BC decree had already done that.
Here is why this reading starts the count with the third line on that chart,
and not the first two.
Daniel 9, 25 asks for a command to restore and to build Jerusalem,
the city, and not the temple only.
Cyrus and Darius gave orders about the temple,
and the Nehemiah permit of 444 BC only let walls be finished under a decree already given.
The seventh-year order to Ezra gave judges,
laws, and punishments, which are the powers of a working city government.
And the building that followed it is what the officials complained about in Ezra 412.
That is why the count starts here.
By the Jewish civil calendar, which began each year in the autumn,
the seventh year of Artaxerxes I, Longamanus,
ran from autumn 458 BC to autumn 457 BC.
Ezra 7, verse 8, says Ezra came to Jerusalem in the fifth month of that seventh year,
so he arrived in the summer of 457 BC.
This reading counts both the 70-week line and the 2300-year line from the autumn of 457 BC,
the first autumn after the decree took effect.
We have come to the first checkpoint.
Main point 3.
The 69 weeks to Messiah, the anointing in AD 27.
Daniel 9, 25 subdivides the 70 weeks into distinct chronological segments,
7 weeks, and 3 score in 2 weeks, 69 weeks, until Messiah the Prince.
7 weeks equal 49 prophetic days, which are 49 solar years,
the time to clear the debris and rebuild Jerusalem's streets and walls in trebleous times.
62 weeks equal 434 prophetic days, which are 434 solar years.
Total, 69 weeks equals 7 plus 62, which is 483 prophetic days, or 483 literal solar years.
The mathematical walk, 457 BC to AD 27, accounting for no year zero.
In historical and astronomical chronology, there is no year zero between BC and AD.
The timeline moves immediately from December 31 BC to January 1 AD 1.
Therefore, when walking across the BC-AD divide,
one year must be added to delete the non-existent zero year.
Negative 457 plus 483 plus 1 equals 27 AD.
Here is the same walk in words, so you can do it yourself.
Start at autumn 457 BC, the autumn the decree took effect.
Count forward 483 whole years.
That count crosses the line between the years before Christ and the years after him,
and because no year zero sits on that line, one year is added back.
483 years, counted from 457 BC, reach 26, and 26 plus the missing year is 27.
So the count lands in autumn AD 27.
It lands in the autumn because a whole number of years counted from an autumn
ends in an autumn, and this reading starts the count in the autumn of 457 BC.
What occurred in autumn AD 27?
Luke 3-1 dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to
the 15th year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar.
Tiberius became emperor in AD 14.
Counting years from autumn to autumn, as the Jews did,
his first year ended in the autumn of AD 14,
so his 15th year began in the autumn of AD 27.
Soon after, Jesus of Nazareth came to the Jordan River to be baptized by John.
As he went up straightway out of the water, Matthew 3-16,
the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the bodily form of a dove,
Luke 3-22, and the Father's voice proclaimed,
Thou art my beloved Son, in thee I am well pleased.
The Hebrew word mashiach, messiah, and the Greek word kristos,
both mean the anointed one.
Luke 2-11 calls him Christ at his birth.
He was anointed for his public mission by the Holy Spirit at his baptism in AD 27,
Acts 10-38.
Daniel 9-25 speaks of the Messiah as he appears to begin his work,
so the anointing at the baptism, not the birth,
is the date that matches.
After 40 days in the wilderness, Mark 1-12-13,
and after John was imprisoned, Mark 1-14,
Jesus entered Galilee preaching the gospel of the kingdom
and proclaiming, the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is at hand.
Repent ye and believe the gospel.
Mark 1-15, KJV.
What time was fulfilled?
Mark does not name Daniel, but this reading hears in Jesus' words
the end of the 69 weeks of Daniel 9-25,
the time set for the arrival of Messiah the prince.
We have come to the second checkpoint.
Main point 4.
The midst of the week, the cross in AD 31 and sacrifices ceasing.
Daniel 9-26-27, Matthew 27-50-51, Hebrews 9-26, and 10-12.
With 69 weeks completed in autumn AD 27,
exactly one prophetic week, seven literal years,
remained of the 70-week covenant allotment.
Daniel 9-26-27 records what transpires in this momentous final week.
And after three score and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself.
And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week,
and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease.
Daniel 9-26-27, KJV.
1. Messiah cut off.
He died in our place.
Daniel 9-26 declares that Messiah would be cut off, but not for himself.
To be cut off is to be put to death, cut off from the living.
The Hebrew phrase, ve'en lo, means that he was not cut off for a crime of his own.
There was no guilt of his own for him to die for.
That is the reason the death was for others.
If it was not for his own sin, then he was bearing the sin of someone else.
He died as an innocent substitute for the sins of the world.
Isaiah 53 verse 5 foretold the same reality.
He was wounded for our transgressions.
He was bruised for our iniquities.
2. The midst of the week, spring AD 31.
The final week of seven years ran from autumn AD 27 to autumn AD 34.
The middle of a seven-year week is three and a half years in,
so three and a half years after autumn AD 27 lands in spring AD 31.
In spring AD 31, at the feast of the Passover, Jesus Christ was crucified on Calvary.
That date follows from counting to the midst of the week in Daniel 9 verse 27,
so it comes from the count itself.
The Gospels fit it.
John mentions Passovers during Jesus' ministry.
John 2 verse 13, 6 verse 4, and 13 verse 1,
which suits a ministry of about three and a half years from his baptism to the last Passover.
3. Causing sacrifices to cease.
The rent veil.
At the exact moment Jesus died on the cross, crying,
it is finished, John 19.30.
The veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom, Matthew 27.51.
The veil hung in the temple between the holy place and the most holy place,
where only the high priest could go.
Its tearing from top to bottom shows that the way to God was now open through Christ.
The earthly sacrifices were a type, a picture pointing ahead to his death,
and the cross is the anti-type, the real thing the picture pointed to.
By offering his own precious blood, once for all,
Jesus brought a permanent end to the divine necessity and efficacy of earthly animal sacrifices,
Hebrews 9 verses 11 through 12, 10 verses 1 through 14.
No ruler issued an order in that hour to stop the temple sacrifices.
The veil tore as he died,
and this reading takes that tearing as the sign that their work was finished.
4. The close of the 70 weeks.
Autumn 8034.
The remaining 3.5 years of the 70th week ran from spring AD 31 to autumn AD 34.
During this period, the disciples wore witness in Jerusalem and in all Judea and in Samaria
and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
Acts 1 verse 8, Acts 8.
Stephen was stoned, Acts 7 verses 54 through 60.
Autumn AD 34 closes the 70th week, 3.5 years after the cross,
as the gospel turns to the wider gentile mission after Stephen, Acts 7 through 8.
The stoning of Stephen closes the 70 weeks allotted to Daniel's people and city,
9 verse 24.
After Stephen's death, the believers were scattered and bore witness beyond Jerusalem,
Acts 8 verses 1 through 4.
Saul of Tarsus was converted on the road to Damascus, Acts 9 verses 1 through 9.
The year AD 34 is an inference from the half week and from Acts,
not a year the text prints.
In plain words, the 70th week is the last 7 years of the 490,
running from the baptism in AD 27 to the autumn of AD 34, with the cross at its middle.
So the 70 weeks are not still waiting to be fulfilled.
On this reading, they finished in the first century,
among Daniel's own people and city.
For a reader today, that means the covenant blessings of the week are already open.
The gospel has gone out to the nations,
and no future 7-year countdown has to start before the prophecy can come true.
Main point 5.
Refuting the dispensationalist gap, Christ confirms the covenant.
Why the 70th week belongs to Jesus, not a future antichrist.
In the 19th century, John Nelson Darby, and later the Scofield Reference Bible,
spread a form of futurism called dispensationalism.
It says the 70th week was cut off from the other 69 and put on hold for more than 2,000 years.
It then expects that week to run in the future as 7 years of great trouble
under one individual antichrist.
People hold that view because they expect a final crisis before Christ returns,
and they look for a place to put it in Daniel.
Its best case is that verse 27 has its own covenant and its own end of sacrifice,
and a gap lets those details land in a still future crisis instead of at the cross.
A second rival reading goes the other way and puts the whole prophecy in the past.
It ends the weeks with the Greek ruler Antiochus,
whose persecution is described outside this chapter,
and with the cleansing of the temple altar in 164 BC.
People hold that reading because the last week's details,
an anointed one cut off, sacrifice stopping, and a desolator
sound like that persecution, and because it keeps the prophecy inside the Old Testament period.
This course answers that Daniel 925 runs the weeks unto the Messiah the Prince,
and 483 years from the decree land in the first century, not the second century BC.
The sacrifices cease here because the true sacrifices come,
not because a foreign king defiled an altar.
But Daniel 9 does not give the gap its place either.
There are four reasons.
Four reasons the gap does not fit Daniel 9.
1. Who is he?
From verse 25 to verse 27, the angel is speaking about one person,
Messiah the Prince in verse 25,
Messiah cut off in verse 26, and then he in verse 27,
and he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week.
The only other figure in verse 26 is the people of the Prince that shall come,
and it is those people who destroy the city, not the Prince.
So he is the Messiah the angel has been following all along, and not a future Antichrist.
A reader might take he to be the Roman general Titus because his troops destroyed the city and
the sanctuary in AD 70, and verse 26 names that destruction just before the word he.
This reading says the destroyers are called the people of the Prince,
not the Prince himself, and the angel has already named Messiah twice, so he is the Messiah.
2. Which covenant is confirmed?
The word Antichrist appears only in John's letters, 1 John 2 18, 22, 4 3, 2 John 7,
and none of those verses speaks of him making a covenant.
In the Bible, the covenant is God's covenant with his people,
and Jesus is the one who confirmed it.
The prophets promised a new covenant, Jeremiah 31 31 to 34,
and Hebrews 8 8 to 13 shows Christ bringing it.
That is the covenant this reading sees in Daniel 9 27.
At the Last Supper, Jesus held the cup and said,
This is my blood of the New Testament which is shed for many for the remission of sins.
Matthew 26 28, Hebrews 8 to 8 to 13.
Testament here means covenant, that is, the agreement between God and his people.
To confirm a covenant is to make it firm, to carry it out so that it stands.
Christ confirmed that covenant through his life and his death.
No verse.
Prince the gap.
Nothing in the text says that the clock stops between the 69th and 70th weeks.
The 70 weeks are given as one block of 490 years that is
determined or cut off, cha-taq, as a single unit.
The gap view takes the 70th week with its covenant and its end of sacrifices away from Jesus
and gives them to a future ruler who is said to make a treaty and then break it.
In this reading, the one who confirms the covenant and causes the sacrifice and the
Jesus himself, and he does it in the middle of the week by dying.
That is the work of Christ on the cross.
4 Why the count carries on to 1844.
Since 490 years of the 2300 year line were completed in 8034,
1810 years remained.
Measuring 1810 years from autumn AD 34 brings us directly to autumn 1844.
34 plus 1810 equals 1844.
The same count has now fit two events in the Gospels.
The baptism in 8027 and the cross in 8031.
So this reading trusts the same count for the rest of the line.
The 1844 end is carried by the count, not by a separate record.
In plain words, the 70 weeks are 490 years from the decree to restore Jerusalem
to the coming of the Messiah, and the cross falls in the middle of the last week.
Interpretation.
Daniel 9 answers the question Daniel 8 left hanging.
Chapter 8 gave a span of 2300 years and no starting point.
And Daniel says plainly that he did not understand it.
Daniel 8 verse 27.
Chapter 9 supplies the start.
And it supplies it in the middle of a prayer about something else.
Gabriel comes back and tells Daniel to consider the vision.
Daniel 9 verse 23.
Then gives him 70 weeks.
Those weeks are 70 times 7, which is 490 days.
Read as literal days, they come to about 16 months,
far too short to rebuild a city, restore a nation, and see the Messiah arrive and die.
Read on the year-day scale, the Bible itself supplies, they are 490 years,
and they run from the decree to restore Jerusalem to the coming of the Messiah.
Three things follow, and this sitting walks each one.
First, the weeks have a starting point in history.
The decree that actually authorized rebuilding the city,
which this reading takes to be the seventh year of Artaxerxes.
Ezra 7.
In 457 BC.
Second, they have a shape.
Seven weeks, then 62 weeks, then one week,
with the Messiah cut off in the middle of that last week.
Third, they have an end.
In AD 34, when the 70 weeks close.
Notice what the arithmetic is doing.
The dates are not the point.
The cross is the point.
And the dates are what make the cross the center of the count.
The one who arranged the return from exile, the rebuilding of the city,
and the arrival of the Messiah is the same God who told Daniel the number in advance.
The bottom line is what the 70th week is and where it ends.
It is not a week still waiting in our future,
separated from the other 69 by a gap no verse prints.
It is the week of the Messiah's own ministry, and its middle is the cross.
Everything the sitting adds, including the reasons the other readings do not fit,
is in service of that one claim, Christ.
Jesus Christ is the divine center of Daniel 9.
He was anointed at the Jordan in AD 27, cut off for our sins at Calvary in AD 31,
and confirmed the everlasting covenant with his own blood.
The cross falls in the middle of the last of the 70 weeks,
so the count has now fit both the baptism and the cross.
This reading therefore carries the same count forward.
The 1,810 years still left after AD 34 and in 1844.
Heavenly sanctuary ministry means Christ's work in heaven as high priest,
the cleansing Daniel 8.14 named, which this reading places at the end of that count.
We have come to the third checkpoint.
